state.misconception_label: Assumes that an arrow on a number line starts at zero

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: ![Number line with -12 and -7 marked. Starting at -12, follow an arrow pointing to the right labelled +10. Then there is an arrow labelled b pointing to the left, which ends at -7 on the number line.]() What is the value of \( b \) ? I got \( -7 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: What would happen if you considered starting the arrow at a different point on the number line?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I guess if I started the arrow at a different point, it could change where it ends up, right? But I thought the arrow always starts at zero, so I'm not sure how that works. Can you explain how to figure out where the arrow starts from?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: What would happen if you considered the possibility that the arrow doesn't always have to start at zero on the number line? How might that change your approach to finding the value of \( b \)?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I get that the arrow can start at different points, not just zero. So if it starts at -12 and goes +10, it would end up at -2, right? But then how do I figure out what \( b \) is from there? I'm still a bit confused about how to follow the arrows correctly.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the zero-starting misconception and the student makes clear progress (correctly calculating -12 + 10 = -2), though the teacher could have provided more concrete scaffolding when the student explicitly requested help in Turn 2, and the student still needs guidance on completing the problem to find b.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking without directly providing answers, perfectly exemplifying the Socratic method by asking 'what would happen if' questions that lead the student to reconsider their assumptions about where arrows start on the number line.
